---

"It's a '49," Rhinehardt said, and slammed
the screen door, then picked his way around
the dog turds in the yard
to the Buick gutted by fire—the gears
teething rust, the fenders sloped
like the shoulders of a fired worker
out of beer. He circled the car,
kicking the tires, eyeing
the grille that still grinned the ribbed wings
of a sparrow. He looked inside, and flies
lifted like patted dust, settling
into a loose knot on the visor.
"Yeah, you're right as right… it's a '50,"
Rhinehardt spat, his tongue rolling
a false tooth into place. "It's got no
running board." He pressed a buck
into his son's hand and retired to the porch,
where he towel-flicked
his wife from a chair,
and as evening came on watched beyond
the street, a kennel of trees,
where—as he had dreamed—a plane would drop
and bloom fire. Two bucks on that one.

---

outputs.L3:
# The Buick

Rhinehardt crouched beside the wreck, his eyes moving slowly over the ruined machine. It had been a Buick once—a 1949 or 1950, he couldn't be certain—but fire had gutted it long ago, leaving behind a carcass of rusted gears and blackened metal. He ran his gaze along the sloping fenders, admiring even now the graceful curve of them, and studied the grille where flecks of chrome still clung stubbornly beneath the corrosion.

The car sat abandoned in a field of neglect. Dog turds littered the ground around the tires, and the whole thing hummed with flies that rose in lazy clouds whenever he shifted his weight, only to settle again moments later upon the cracked visor. The smell of decay and old rain hung in the air, thick and unmoving.

He lingered over the question of the model year, turning it in his mind the way a man turns a coin. A '49 or a '50—it mattered to him, though he could not have said why. Finally he leaned down and checked the side. No running board. That settled it.

"A '50," he said aloud, satisfied.

Rising, Rhinehardt reached into his pocket and pressed a dollar into his son's hand without a word of explanation. Then he made his way back toward the house and up onto the porch. His wife sat in the good chair. He flicked a towel at her, casually, as though shooing one of the flies, and she got up and moved aside to let him take her place.

He settled in as the light began to fail. The evening came down soft over the yard, and he watched the trees stand black against the fading sky. In his mind a plane appeared, droning low, and he pictured it clipping the treetops and going down—the sudden bloom of fire, the beautiful violence of it.

"Two dollars says it happens," he murmured to no one, and kept his eyes fixed on the darkening trees, waiting.
outputs.L4:
# The Buick

The yard sprawled behind the chain-link fence like something the world had forgotten, a graveyard of steel and rust where sunlight came to die. Rhinehardt moved through it slowly, his boots crunching over broken glass and the brittle skeletons of things once useful. Everywhere lay the debris of abandoned ambition: cracked engine blocks, tangled wire like nests of metal snakes, the hollow shells of appliances rotting back into the earth.

He stopped before the Buick.

Fire had taken it, and taken it thoroughly. The paint had blistered and peeled away to reveal the scorched bones beneath, black and flaking. The seats were gutted, springs exposed like the ribs of some great animal picked clean by scavengers. The windows had exploded outward long ago, leaving only jagged teeth of glass in the frames. Yet Rhinehardt studied it with the reverence of a man appraising a masterpiece.

"Fifty-three," he said, running a blackened finger along the curve of the fender.

His son shook his head. "Fifty-one. Look at the grille."

"That's a fifty-three grille if I ever saw one."

"Twenty says it isn't."

Rhinehardt smiled, a thin crack in the weathered map of his face. "Fifty, then. Fifty says you're wrong, and I'm the one who's right." He spat into the dirt. "You always did have a bad eye for these things."

The boy laughed, but there was something careful in it, something learned. He had grown up in yards like this, among the wreckage, watching his father wager on the fall of every card life dealt. It was the only faith Rhinehardt had ever passed down—not hope, not God, but the odds. Everything was a bet. Every ruin held a number, and every number held a chance.

They circled the car together, arguing model years, trading dollars neither of them could spare. The afternoon stretched long and yellow around them. And as Rhinehardt talked, his eyes drifted upward, past the fence, past the smokestacks bleeding gray into a bruised sky.

He saw it then, though it wasn't there.

A plane, silver and small, tilting from the clouds. He watched it fall the way he watched everything fall—without alarm, without prayer, only the calm arithmetic of a man who had seen too much collapse to be surprised by more. It dropped soundlessly in his mind, nose down, and bloomed into a flower of orange fire against the horizon. He felt nothing. He had felt nothing for a long time.

"You see that?" the boy asked, following his father's gaze.

"Nothing there," Rhinehardt said. "Just thinking."

But he kept watching the empty sky, the imagined flames folding into the real smoke of the factories, all of it one great burning to him now—the car, the yard, the plane, the years. He had bet his whole life against the house and lost, and the losing had emptied him out until only the calculation remained.

"Fifty-three," he said again, quietly, as if the argument mattered, as if anything did. "I'd stake my life on it."

The boy pulled a crumpled bill from his pocket and pressed it into his father's waiting palm, and somewhere beyond the fence the sun went down like a coin swallowed by the dark.
outputs.L5:
# The Rhinehardt Buick

Old Man Rhinehardt loved that Buick more than anything else in the world. It sat in his driveway like a monument to another era—all polished chrome and deep burgundy paint that caught the morning sun just right.

"They don't make cars like this anymore," he'd tell anyone who'd listen. And he was right. The Buick had rolled off the assembly line back in 1965, and Rhinehardt had been its only owner ever since.

Every Sunday, without fail, he would wash and wax the vehicle in his driveway, humming old tunes while the water beaded on the flawless surface. The neighborhood kids would gather at the fence, marveling at the classic beauty that seemed to belong in a museum rather than an ordinary suburban street.

The Buick had seen him through everything—his wedding day, when he'd nervously driven to the church; the long trips to the hospital when his wife fell ill; and the quiet drives afterward, when the passenger seat sat empty and the silence felt heavier than the steel of the old machine.

When Rhinehardt finally passed away at ninety-two, his grandson inherited the car. He understood immediately why his grandfather had cherished it so. The Buick wasn't just an automobile—it was a rolling collection of memories, a testament to a life well-lived.

And so the tradition continued. Every Sunday morning, the Rhinehardt Buick still gleams in the driveway, its legacy polished bright for another generation to admire.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a narrative poem about an old man named Rhinehardt inspecting a rusted-out Buick in his junky yard while betting with his son.
counterfactuals.output:
# Rhinehardt's Wager

The morning came up copper through the weeds
where Rhinehardt walked his acre lot of rust,
past axles bent like question marks, past seeds
of dandelions rising through the dust
of engines that had died a decade back.
His son came trailing, hands shoved deep in jeans.
"That Buick there," the old man said, "is black
beneath the orange. Fifty-four, I mean."

"You're guessing, Pop." The boy kicked at a tire
that crumbled soft as ash beneath his boot.
"I'll bet you twenty says the whole front's wire
and rot. No engine block. No parts to loot."
The old man crouched, his knees a symphony
of pops and protests, laid his weathered palm
against the fender, closed his eyes to see
the way a blind man reads a psalm.

"Your grandfather could name a car by sound,
by smell, by how the shadow crossed the hood.
This here's a straight-eight, buried in the ground
of forty years. She ran. She ran up good."
He pulled the latch. It shrieked but gave its ghost—
and there, beneath the dirt-daubers and grime,
the engine sat, intact, a rusted host
that still remembered turning, keeping time.

The boy leaned in. His smart mouth fell to still.
"I'll be damned, Pop." He fished the twenty out.
But Rhinehardt shook his head against the bill.
"Keep it. I didn't teach you this to doubt
the thing your hands can know when eyes can't tell.
Some men see junk. Some men see what it was."
He wiped his hands. The morning rang a bell
of distant church. He smiled. "Just like it does."

They stood together in the rising heat,
two shadows thrown across the ruined chrome,
the father old, the son not yet complete,
and all around them, cars that wouldn't roam
lay rusting into earth, becoming ground—
but in that yard where broken things were kept,
an old man taught his boy what could be found,
and something in the son's proud silence, wept.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a gritty free-verse poem in the style of Gary Soto about working-class life, an abandoned car, and a father's strange daydreams.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Buick in the Weeds

My father kept a dead car
behind the house, a Buick
the color of a bruise,
tires flat as old tortillas,
the hood open like a mouth
that forgot how to speak.

He worked the canneries then,
came home smelling of fish
and machine oil, his hands
cracked into little rivers
that never ran clean.
But Sundays he'd walk out
to that Buick, sit inside
where the seats had split
and spilled their yellow foam,
and just hold the wheel.

I watched from the window.
He wasn't going anywhere.
The engine was a nest
for mice and rust,
but his lips moved
like a man reading a map
of some other country,
somewhere the roads
were paved with second chances.

Once I asked him where.
He said *Fresno, maybe.
Or the moon.*
Then he laughed that laugh
that wasn't quite a laugh,
more like the sound
a tired thing makes
before it starts again.

My mother called us in.
Beans on the stove,
the radio spitting static
and a distant baseball game.
He came, he always came,
but part of him stayed out there,
hands on a wheel that turned
nothing but the years,
driving through the weeds
toward a horizon
only he could see,
the one the paycheck
never let us reach.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem set in a poor neighborhood where a man argues about the year of a burned car, hands his son a dollar, and imagines a plane crashing into the trees at dusk.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Year of the Burned Car

On Delancey where the hydrants weep
their rust into the gutter's throat,
two men lean close above the wreck—
a Chevy, maybe, someone's ghost

of chrome and cinder. *Seventy-nine,*
one swears, and jabs a blackened door.
*The hell it is. That's eighty-two.*
As if it mattered anymore

what year the fire took its shape,
what year the wheels forgot to turn.
The argument is something warm
to hold, a small thing left to burn.

The boy stands quiet by his father's hip,
half-listening, kicking at a can.
The man breaks off. He digs one hand
into the pocket of his worn-out pants

and finds a dollar, soft as cloth,
and folds it in the small brown fist.
*Go on. Get something.* And the boy
runs light, as if he won't be missed,

past the liquor store, the boarded church,
the block dissolving into blue.
The father watches, and the dusk
comes down the way that dusk will do—

and something in him lifts its eyes
above the roofline, past the wires,
to where a plane hangs low and slow,
its belly gilded by the fires

of evening, and he sees it dip,
he lets it fall inside his mind
into the far-off row of trees,
a silent blossom, undefined—

not wishing it, exactly. Just
the way a man will hold a thing
he cannot name against the ache,
the way he'll watch a burning wing

and feel the argument dissolve,
the year unmatter, the boy return
with candy melting in his palm,
the streetlights, one by one, unlearn

the dark. He takes his son's free hand.
The plane climbs safe into the night.
The car stays burned. Whatever year.
They walk home slowly, out of sight.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a vivid, image-heavy poem featuring dog turds, a fire-gutted 1949 or 1950 Buick, flies on a visor, and a man who bets money with his son.
counterfactuals.output:
**Vacant Lot, End of August**

The dog turds have gone gray as knuckles
in the weeds, curled and cracking
where the heat has had its way with them,
little monuments the flies abandoned
for the visor of the Buick—

a '49, maybe '50, hard to say
now that the fire took the badges
and the chrome went the color of a burnt match.
The upholstery is a black lung.
The steering wheel a licorice ring
somebody left too near the stove.

On the visor the flies do their arithmetic,
green-backed, rubbing their hands
like men who have already won,
crawling the melted lip of shade
that is the only shade for a mile.

And here comes the father,
belly first, dollar bills soft as cloth
from the wash, folding one lengthwise,
snapping it flat against his thigh.

*Ten says you can't hit the hood ornament.*

The boy has a fistful of gravel
and the whole afternoon in his arm.
*Ten,* he says, and doesn't blink,
and the father grins his brown grin
and lays the bill on the fender
where the paint has blistered up
in bubbles you could pop with a thumbnail.

The stone goes wide. The flies lift once,
a small dark applause, and settle.
The father takes his ten back slow,
the way a man takes what was always his,

and the dog turds keep their counsel
in the weeds, gray as knuckles,
gray as the Buick, gray as the coin
of light the boy has just been taught
he cannot spend.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short poem about masculinity, poverty, and dark imagination, centered on a character named Rhinehardt who studies a ruined car and dreams of fire falling from the sky.
counterfactuals.output:
# Rhinehardt and the Rust

The car sits dead in the yellow grass,
a carcass Rhinehardt learned to read—
each rusted seam, each shatter of glass
a scripture of some slower creed.

He is a man because the men
before him named the thing a man:
hard hands, hard jaw, and now and then
the ache of doing what he can.

The engine block will never turn.
The paycheck thins to paper-white.
So Rhinehardt lets the whole world burn
inside the theater of his mind at night—

a rain of fire, a falling sky,
the county lit like judgment day,
the mill, the bank, the reasons why,
all glowing red and burned away.

Not cruelty. Just a boy who found
no other door the world would give,
and so he salvaged, underground,
a darker way to dream, and live—

and every morning stands to face
the wreck, the field, the empty road,
and wears his hunger like a grace,
and hauls again the daily load.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
